precepts.text: If he beget a son that seeth all his father's sins which he hath done, and considereth, and doeth not such like: a son can see it and change.
precepts.point: As I live, saith the Lord God, ye shall not have occasion any more to use this proverb. The Lord is saying: I am not letting you use intergenerational trauma as your excuse.

note.label: Shapen in Iniquity: Resetting the Nervous System

precepts.why:
The proverb was, “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge”: the present generation punished for the offences of their forefathers. The people were prone to plead their innocence: listen, I am this way because my father was this way. But the Lord said, “ye shall not have occasion any more to use this proverb in Israel.” I am not letting you use the fact that you have been through intergenerational trauma, or that your fathers weren't right.

“Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die.” From here on out, you are not going to say, well, my daddy was wicked, so I am just going to be wicked by default. No, you are going to change it.

Verse 14 shows the son who does: “Now, lo, if he beget a son, that seeth all his father’s sins which he hath done, and considereth, and doeth not such like”. The son sees everything his father did, considers it, and does not do the same. A son can see it and change.

So the proverb is broken by a son who looks at his father's ways with open eyes. The iniquity we were shapen in is real, but it is not a sentence we have to serve; the son who considers and does not do such like is the proof that it can be changed.

Intergenerational trauma is real; but do you sit in it, or do you change? Just because our fathers were wicked, and our mothers did not know God's laws, that is not an excuse to stay in this. note.label: Shapen in Iniquity: Resetting the Nervous System

precepts.why:
The people still asked, “Yet say ye, Why? doth not the son bear the iniquity of the father?” That is the sour grapes proverb again. The Lord answers: “When the son hath done that which is lawful and right, and hath kept all my statutes, and hath done them, he shall surely live. The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father”.

In other words, yes, intergenerational trauma is real. But do you just sit in it, or do you change? This son changed. If there is a son who changes and does what is right according to the Lord, he is not going to die, although his father will. Just because our fathers were wicked, just because our mothers didn't know God's laws and taught us evil, that is not an excuse to stay in this. That trauma is real; you must recognise it and move on from it.

“neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.” Each soul answers for itself.

And the Lord still has mercy on the sick. Christ said, “They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick”, and “I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” That is every last one of us. Although we have been through trauma and traumatic experiences, we cannot use the excuse of what we have been through anymore. Christ has given us a clean slate, and the way to walk in it is to keep his statutes and do them.

precepts.text: A just man is one that does that which is lawful and right.
precepts.point: Lot was a just man. To be just means to do that which is lawful and right, a commandment keeper; righteous Lot was vexed from day to day with the unlawful deeds of the wicked.

note.label: Genesis 11: Babel and the Separation of the Nations

precepts.why:
Haran begat Lot, and Lot was a just man. What just means: “But if a man be just, and do that which is lawful and right.”

To be just is to do that which is lawful and right, a commandment keeper. That is the Lot who went forth with Terah and Abram from Ur of the Chaldees, Ur meaning fire and the Chaldees being Babylon, the area Abram was born in and called out of.

precepts.text: The soul that sinneth, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.
precepts.point: The soul that sinneth, it shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
“The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.”

That is this law in the prophet: every man put to death for his own sin, and no other man's. The son does not carry the father's iniquity, nor the father the son's; each man's righteousness or wickedness is upon himself.

precepts.text: If he beget a son that is a robber, a shedder of blood, that lifts up his eyes to the idols and commits abomination, he shall not live: he hath done all these abominations; he shall surely die; his blood shall be upon him. The son that continues in the sins of his father dies for his own doings.
precepts.point: Why would the Lord judge the children of future generations of Eli's house? The thought might be, he is killing them for the sins of their forefather; I thought the sons did not die for the fathers. Ezekiel 18 shows what it is talking about: the judgment falls on the son that continues in the sins of his father.

note.label: 1 Samuel 2: By Him Actions Are Weighed

precepts.why:
“I will cut off thine arm, and the arm of thy father’s house, that there shall not be an old man in thine house.” Cutting off the arm means cutting off thy strength, and it was talking about his children. The Lord was going to kill Eli's descendants young: “all the increase of thine house shall die in the flower of their age”, in the full strength and peak of their youth.

Why would the Lord judge the children of future generations of Eli's house? The thought might be, he is killing them for the sins of their forefather; I thought the sons did not die for the fathers. Ezekiel 18 shows what it is talking about: “If he beget a son that is a robber, a shedder of blood”, that “hath lifted up his eyes to the idols, hath committed abomination”: “shall he then live? he shall not live: he hath done all these abominations; he shall surely die; his blood shall be upon him.”

The judgment falls on the son that continues in the sins of his father, and he dies for his own doings. Eli's descendants were going to follow in the same way of their fathers, the sons of Belial, doing wickedness and evil. Because Eli did not reprove his sons, the generations after would follow right in their footsteps.

precepts.text: But if he beget a son that seeth all his father's sins which he hath done, and considereth, and doeth not such like, he shall not die for the iniquity of his father; he shall surely live. Eating upon the mountains is partaking in the heathen's idol worship, the food and the drink that went into it, as when Israel rose up to eat and to play before the calf.
precepts.point: Why would the Lord judge the children of future generations of Eli's house? The thought might be, he is killing them for the sins of their forefather; I thought the sons did not die for the fathers. note.label: 1 Samuel 2: By Him Actions Are Weighed

precepts.why:
“Now, lo, if he beget a son, that seeth all his father’s sins which he hath done, and considereth, and doeth not such like”, “he shall not die for the iniquity of his father, he shall surely live.”

Eating upon the mountains is partaking in the heathen's idol worship, the food and the drink that went into it, as when Israel rose up to eat and to play before the calf. The son who “hath not eaten upon the mountains, neither hath lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel”, who “hath executed my judgments, hath walked in my statutes”, lives.

So the cutting off of Eli's house was not the sons dying for the father. The Lord cut them off in the strength of their youth because they were going to follow in the same way of their fathers.

precepts.text: If the wicked turn from all his sins and keep the statutes, he shall surely live, and his transgressions shall not be mentioned unto him.
precepts.point: But Christ told us if we keep the commandments and follow him, we will rule on thrones with him, so there is falsehood in Eliphaz's answer.

note.label: Job 22: Acquaint Now Thyself With Him

precepts.why:
“But if the wicked will turn from all his sins that he hath committed, and keep all my statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die. All his transgressions that he hath committed, they shall not be mentioned unto him: in his righteousness that he hath done he shall live.” Keeping the statutes profits: it is life, and the transgressions are not mentioned.

Eliphaz says, “Is not thy wickedness great? and thine iniquities infinite?”, as if righteousness gains a man nothing before the Almighty. But the Most High says the man that turns and keeps all his statutes shall surely live, in his righteousness that he hath done. So keeping the commandments is not filthy rags, and there is falsehood in Eliphaz's answer.

precepts.text: If a man be just and do that which is lawful and right; not everybody can keep the commandments, only Israel, repented Israel, which is what makes us just.
precepts.point: He may prepare it, but the just shall put it on and the innocent shall divide the silver; we do not want their Louis Vuitton, Versace, or Hermes bags, we want our kingdom back and the whole earth, because it belongs to us, plus what they took and some.

note.label: Job 27: I Will Not Remove My Integrity From Me

precepts.why: Who is the just that shall put on the raiment and divide the silver? “But if a man be just, and do that which is lawful and right”. The just is the one who does that which is lawful and right, and not everybody can keep the commandments. Only Israel, repented Israel, and that is what makes us just. The wicked of our own people get no pass; it is the ones who do that which is lawful and right who receive what the wicked prepared.

precepts.text: The just man that doeth that which is lawful and right is the picture of this righteous cell.
precepts.point: These attributes are the same standard laid out in the law and in the description of the just, righteous man.

note.label: Psalm 15: Who Shall Abide in the Tabernacle

precepts.why:
“But if a man be just, and do that which is lawful and right”. The just man that doeth that which is lawful and right is the picture of this righteous man: one who backbiteth not with his tongue, does no evil to his neighbour, takes up no reproach against him, contemns the vile person but honours them that fear the Lord, sweareth to his own hurt and changeth not, puts not out his money to usury nor takes reward against the innocent.

These attributes are the same standard laid out in the law and in the description of the just, righteous man. “He that doeth these things shall never be moved.”

precepts.text: The Most High judges the house of Israel every one according to his ways, and calls them to repent and turn from all transgressions so that iniquity is not their ruin.
precepts.point: "Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord." People say they repented without understanding the scriptural meaning of the words. To repent is to turn from all your transgressions, and to be converted is to change, which requires the law to change to.

note.label: Acts 3: The Restitution of All Things

precepts.why:
People say they repented without understanding the scriptural meaning of the word. Ezekiel gives it: “Therefore I will judge you, O house of Israel, every one according to his ways, saith the Lord God. Repent, and turn yourselves from all your transgressions; so iniquity shall not be your ruin.”

To repent is to turn from all your transgressions. The Most High judges the house of Israel every one according to his ways, and calls them to turn so that iniquity is not their ruin. That is what Peter is telling the same house of Israel: repent, so that your sins may be blotted out.

precepts.text: To repent is to turn yourselves from all your transgressions, cast away your breaking of the laws, and make you a new heart and a new spirit, so iniquity will not be your ruin.
precepts.point: As yet the Holy Ghost was fallen upon none of them; only they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. They first had to believe in Christ in the place of animal sacrifice, believing that Christ could forgive sins when Moses' sacrifices could not. The subject matter of that day was the law and animal sacrifice versus the name of Jesus Christ, which is why the apostles keep saying to repent and believe in his name.

note.label: Acts 8: The Word Scattered Abroad, and the Baptism unto the Conscience

precepts.why:
What is it to repent? “Repent, and turn yourselves from all your transgressions; so iniquity shall not be your ruin. Cast away from you all your transgressions, whereby ye have transgressed; and make you a new heart and a new spirit: for why will ye die, O house of Israel?” To repent is to turn yourselves from all your transgressions, cast away your breaking of the laws, and make you a new heart and a new spirit, so iniquity will not be your ruin.

“Therefore I will judge you, O house of Israel, every one according to his ways, saith the Lord God.” This is spoken to the house of Israel. So when the apostles say repent and believe in his name, repentance is turning from breaking the laws, and the name of Jesus Christ is what takes the place of animal sacrifice for the forgiveness of the sin.

points: Cast away all your transgressions and make you a new heart and a new spirit, the heart being the mind, for the Most High has no pleasure in the death of him that dies; wherefore turn yourselves and live.
